title: Gordon Street mixed-use apartment approval
subtitle: Also: Victoria Road North townhouse rezoning, two heritage decisions, and a firefighters agreement ratified in closed session.
overview: Council approved an Official Plan amendment and zoning changes for a four to seven storey mixed-use building at 1373 and 1389 Gordon Street {{vote:m6}}. It will have 99 apartment units and 850 square metres of commercial space. The applicant said the units will be purpose-built rental. The design was reduced from an earlier, taller proposal after the applicant met with a neighbourhood group.

On the consent agenda, Council approved rezoning at 103-105 Victoria Road North for stacked and cluster townhouses and three single detached homes {{vote:m5}}. It removed 20 Cityview Drive North from the heritage register and approved demolition of its barn {{vote:m3}}. It also began the process to designate 49 Norfolk Street as a heritage property {{vote:m4}}.

After a closed session, the Mayor said Council supported ratifying a Memorandum of Agreement with the Guelph Professional Firefighters Union Local 467 and gave staff direction. Staff also announced a coming workshop on the housing crisis, where the City plans to share its work and discuss options within its control.

decisions.detail: Council approved an Official Plan amendment and zoning changes for a four to seven storey mixed-use building with 99 apartments and 850 square metres of commercial space.
Council approved rezoning to allow 32 stacked townhouses, 23 cluster townhouses and 3 single detached dwellings, with no further public notice needed for minor changes.
Council removed the property from the Municipal Register of Cultural Heritage Properties and approved demolition of the barn.
Council authorized notice of intention to designate the property under the Ontario Heritage Act, with a designation by-law to follow if no objections are received in 30 days.

debate: A delegate raised an apparent contradiction on sewer capacity: a servicing report mentioned downstream constraints, while the staff report said capacity was sufficient. Staff said the applicant's wording was out of date, since Council approved updated wastewater and sanitary master plans in April, and engineering had signed off.

One councillor asked about stormwater and flooding risk, noting a nearby road floods regularly. The applicant's representative said the high groundwater level had been studied and expected no stormwater issues, though no engineer was present.

Councillors asked about parking, which fell by about 30 spaces from the earlier design. The applicant called it a balance with shared visitor and commercial spaces. Staff said the April zoning change applied to apartment buildings only, and this mixed-use proposal falls within the parking range set for its area. One councillor remained concerned about overflow parking.

A councillor asked about a signalized crossing at Gordon Street and the intersection near the site. Staff said an October traffic survey met no warrants for a signal, so the intersection will be roughed in during Gordon Street improvements and reviewed if warrants are met.

Supporters pointed to the lower height, changes made after community meetings, added common amenity space, a public trail connection and environmental features such as possible solar panels. They said these helped housing and climate goals. The applicant said the building will not have specifically wheelchair-accessible units but will be visitable throughout.
